analysis.one_liner: Guarantees people with disabilities who need long-term care the right to live at home instead of institutions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced and died there with no hearing, markup, or vote, despite 10 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal discrimination for states, local governments, and insurers to push people with disabilities who qualify for institutional care into nursing homes and other institutions when home- and community-based services could let them live independently. States would have to plan and report on a transition out of institutional care over 12 years, ensure enough accessible affordable housing, and could earn a 5-percentage-point boost in federal Medicaid matching money for home and community-based services by complying. Individuals could sue, and the Justice Department could enforce the law with penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need help with daily living or health-related tasks and are in an institution or at risk of being placed in one. They would gain an enforceable federal right to receive community-based services — help at home, transportation, integrated housing — instead of being institutionalized, with the option to sue and recover damages. Family caregivers would gain support programs, and low-income disabled people would gain priority for accessible, affordable housing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled people in or facing institutions

how_it_helps.text: Bars states, local governments, and insurers from denying community-based long-term services to people eligible for institutional placement, including through cost caps, waiting lists, restrictive eligibility rules, or requirements that services be delivered in congregate settings.

Requires that community-based services be offered before anyone is institutionalized, and that people already in institutions be regularly notified of community alternatives and receive them if they choose.

Requires states, working with housing agencies, to ensure enough affordable, accessible, integrated housing so people can actually choose to live in the community, with priority for the lowest-income individuals.

Creates an enforceable private right: individuals could sue in federal court for actual and punitive damages and injunctions, with possible court-appointed counsel, and the Justice Department could investigate and seek civil penalties of up to $100,000 for a first violation.
Rewards states that comply by raising their federal Medicaid match by 5 percentage points for home and community-based service spending, lowering the state share of the transition.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments that fund institutional placements would face new obligations to shift money from institutions to home- and community-based care, build accessible housing, and pay rates adequate to sustain a home-care workforce, partially offset by the 5-point Medicaid match bonus. Private long-term care insurers would be barred from denying or limiting community-based services their policyholders qualify for and would be exposed to lawsuits. Nursing homes and other institutional providers would lose residents and funding as states shift spending to community care.

drawbacks.text: Full compliance would not be required until 12 years after enactment, so people stuck in institutions could wait more than a decade for the promise to be fully realized.

The transition would cost states and insurers real money: the bill requires payment rates sufficient to sustain a home-care workforce, while the 5-point Medicaid match bonus lasts only 10 years and goes only to states found to be complying with their transition plans.

The bill tightly limits what counts as community living, capping group residences at 4 unrelated people and barring disability-specific settings, which would eliminate larger group homes some residents and families prefer.
New liability for insurers and expanded enforcement could raise long-term care insurance premiums and invite litigation over what services states must fund.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with disabilities facing institutionalization, the stakes are freedom and family life, and the bill would have turned an unfulfilled ADA promise into an enforceable right backed by money and courts. The honest costs are real but bounded: states would need to restructure long-term care spending over a 12-year runway, with federal matching money to help, and private insurers would take on new coverage duties. The main design weakness is the slow timeline and the tight limits on congregate settings, which could leave some people with fewer options during and after the transition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the Disability Integration Act of 2015 on December 18, 2015, near the end of the first session of the 114th Congress.
That same day the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The action history shows no further steps of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2017.

The bill attracted 10 cosponsors: 9 of the Senate's 44 Democrats and 1 of its 2 Independents, with no Republican support, which was far short of what would be needed to move a bill through a committee chaired by the Republican majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States, insurers, and institutional care providers kept the existing arrangement intact, in which people who qualify for institutional care can be steered into nursing facilities without being guaranteed home- and community-based alternatives. Disabled Americans in or at risk of institutional placement gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Institutional care providers and states kept the status quo

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it expire there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was never voted on, so no vote split exists; its support leaned Democratic — 9 of 44 Democrats and 1 of 2 Independents signed on, with none of the 54 Republicans cosponsoring — but it was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities and other institutional care providers
industries.note: The bill requires states to offer community-based services before institutionalization and to shift funding from institutional settings to integrated community care, moving residents and Medicaid dollars away from nursing facilities. Its revenue model depends on the institutional placement the bill curtails.

Private insurers that fund long-term services would be barred from denying community-based services to policyholders eligible for institutional care, including through cost caps and waiting lists, and would face DOJ enforcement and civil suits with damages.

industries.industry: Home care and community-based service providers
industries.note: A federal right to community-based services, plus required payment rates sufficient to sustain a workforce, would expand demand for home health aides, personal care, and community support services. The bill grows this industry's customer base and codifies its role as the alternative to institutions.

States would take on binding transition plans, housing guarantees, and reporting duties, but would also gain a 5-percentage-point increase in the federal Medicaid match for home and community-based services while complying, and could reduce spending on institutional care over time.
